title: Looking ahead: Why lab-enabled gaps in care strategies need to start planning now for 2027 quality performance
summary: Electronic health records integrations with genetic testing increases operational efficiency, enhances the provider experience and offers precision medicine at scale.
body_markdown:
## *Executive Summary*


The NCQA’s proposed HEDIS® measurement year (MY) 2027 updates are expected to reshape quality performance measures across CMS Star Ratings, Medicaid quality programs, and value-based performance. As those requirements evolve, lab data has become a critical source of evidence that confirms screenings, supports chronic-condition monitoring, and demonstrates care gaps have been closed.


This article explores how year-round lab-enabled gaps in care strategies can help organizations identify opportunities earlier, improve quality performance, and enhance population health. It also details how lab data enables segmented outreach, reduces operational strain, and helps you reach vulnerable populations with measurable action throughout the year.


August has become an important planning milestone for health plans and risk-bearing provider organizations as they begin preparing for the following year's strategic, operational, and financial priorities. Each year, the NCQA's proposed HEDIS updates provide an early view of where quality measurement is headed, helping organizations assess emerging requirements, prioritize resources, and prepare for future performance expectations.


For organizations focused on Medicare Advantage (MA), Medicaid, commercial quality programs, and value-based care, these updates reinforce a broader reality: quality success is increasingly driven by timely clinical data, earlier intervention, and year-round engagement rather than late-year gap closure campaigns.


The NCQA's HEDIS measurement year (MY) 2027 updates continue this evolution.[Measures proposed in August](https://www.ncqa.org/blog/hedis-my-2027-whats-new-whats-changed-whats-retired/) of 2026 address:


- Person-centered outcomes
- Prenatal syphilis screenings
- Continuous glucose monitoring utilization
- Follow-up after positive colorectal cancer screenings


The NCQA also continues its transition toward Electronic Clinical Data Systems (ECDS) reporting and digital quality measurement with ongoing efforts to reduce administrative burden and improve the use of interoperable clinical data.


At the same time, CMS continues to emphasize quality accountability across programs. The 2026 MA star ratings will affect 2027 quality bonus payments, with CMS projecting a 2.48% net average increase in the calendar year, as[2027 MA and Part D policies](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/contract-year-2027-medicare-advantage-part-d-final-rule) continue to position quality performance as a core driver of reimbursement and plan competitiveness.


CMS is also evaluating MA plans across as many as[43 measures for MA-PD contracts and 33 measures for MA-only contracts](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/contract-year-2027-medicare-advantage-part-d-final-rule) . For Medicaid organizations, the shift is equally significant.


[CMS requires states](https://www.medicaid.gov/federal-policy-guidance/downloads/sho25005.pdf) to establish a Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Quality Rating System with mandatory quality measure ratings displayed publicly no later than Dec. 31, 2028. Across the board, quality performance is becoming more transparent, standardized, and visible to beneficiaries, providers, and regulators.


Because of this backdrop, it’s increasingly necessary to have a year-round operational strategy for gaps in care programs to meet quality measures, replacing traditional year-end interventions.


## The case for moving gaps in care programs earlier in the year


The 2027 HEDIS updates present the perfect opportunity for year-round gaps in care strategies, especially with their emphasis on person-centered outcomes and continuous glucose monitoring. Late-year outreach for any measures creates operational strain that ripples across your whole organization, compressing months of work into weeks, and providers field last-minute requests for records.


Members also get bombarded with redundant reminders, affecting engagement and satisfaction. Hard-to-reach populations, who already face the greatest barriers to preventive screening and chronic-condition monitoring, get less time to respond.


## Lab data supports both identification and validation


Organizations need reliable ways to identify members who still require clinical action and verify when care has already occurred. As HEDIS continues its transition toward digital quality measurement and expanded ECDS reporting, source-backed clinical data becomes increasingly valuable as it emphasizes interoperability, electronic clinical data, and reduced dependence on labor-intensive reporting approaches.


Lab-driven intervention changes the math. Outreach can be segmented by population, risk, barriers, and preferred access channels.


Completions and results flow back through reporting, which lets quality teams monitor progress and reprioritize throughout the year instead of all at once. That continuous loop is what turns gaps in care from a year-end campaign into a year-round quality performance lever.


Lab data supports many quality measures that influence performance and population health. Screening and monitoring activities tied to diabetes, kidney health, cardiovascular disease, colorectal cancer screening, hepatitis testing, and broader preventive care all rely on accurate clinical evidence to identify eligible members, complete testing, confirm results, and support reporting.


Several of the new and updated measures touch the exact clinical territory where lab data does its quiet work:


- The continuous glucose monitoring utilization measure brings diabetes management into sharper focus by helping to manage glucose trends, respond to hypoglycemic events and reduce the risk of serious diabetes-related complications
- NCQA is allowing voluntary ECDS reporting for the glycemic status assessment for patients with diabetes
- Follow-up after positive colorectal cancer noninvasive screening tests tracks colonoscopy completion after a positive noninvasive screen for people 45-75
- Prenatal syphilis measure tracks screening tests during the first trimester or within 14 days of the first pregnancy diagnosis or prenatal visit or within 30 days of enrollment
- Several cardiovascular and diabetes measures that track blood pressure and A1c are moving toward ECDS-only reporting, with hybrid methods slated for removal by MY 2029


Lab results are often evidence for open gaps related to diabetes management, kidney health evaluation, cardiovascular risk management, colorectal cancer screening, and preventive testing. This evidence can also help validate test completion and provide documentation that supports quality reporting workflows.


Without the data that lab results can provide, a completed test can look like an open gap and an open gap can stay hidden until late in the year. For quality leaders, getting these insights earlier creates better visibility into performance throughout the year rather than when reporting deadlines approach.


## Building readiness for digital quality measurement


Another reason to shift gaps in care programs earlier is the ongoing transition toward digital quality measurement as NCQA continues to expand ECDS reporting and digital measurement capabilities across multiple clinical domains.


Electronic lab reports and interoperable clinical data are increasingly recognized as important sources for quality measurement. NCQA's long-term vision includes more automated, prospective, and clinically integrated quality reporting models.


Organizations that establish strong lab data workflows today may be better positioned to support future HEDIS reporting requirements, ECDS measures, race and ethnicity stratifications, and emerging digital quality initiatives.


Preparation for 2027 quality performance is not limited to identifying gaps. It also includes strengthening the data foundation needed to measure, monitor, and demonstrate improvement.


## Turning lab insights into measurable action


The organizations that tend to perform well on quality measures treat gap closure as a process, not an event. An effective year-round quality improvement framework typically includes several connected steps:


- Use lab and population data to identify priority members and measures, prioritize timely interventions, and confirm gaps that have already been completed through historical data
- Focus on preventive screening and chronic-condition monitoring opportunities
- Segment outreach based on risk, geography, access barriers, and engagement preferences
- Deploy in-person testing, at-home kits, or hybrid testing options
- Support members through reminders and patient service resources
- Track completion rates and results through reporting and analytics
- Share actionable data that supports provider follow-up, documentation, quality reporting, and future program optimization


Each step builds on the last. Earlier identification supports better prioritization. Better prioritization supports more targeted outreach. More targeted outreach supports higher completion rates. Clean, interoperable lab data supports the ECDS reporting that increasingly underpins HEDIS.


This model works across lines of business, geographies, and provider networks, which matters for organizations juggling MA, Medicaid, commercial, and value-based care performance simultaneously. It also creates a more sustainable model for quality performance than year-end outreach efforts alone.


## Flexible access helps reduce member barriers


Many vulnerable and hard-to-reach populations face practical barriers that make test completion difficult. This is especially true for preventive care like prenatal syphilis screening or seemingly nonurgent measures like continuous glucose monitoring.


Transportation challenges, work schedules, caregiving responsibilities, geographic distance, and fragmented care access can all contribute to lower screening and monitoring rates. A successful gaps in care strategy incorporates convenient testing pathways aligning with member preferences and circumstances.


Depending on population needs, programs may include at-home testing, patient service center access, or hybrid engagement models. This flexibility supports underserved populations while helping organizations improve screening completion rates across multiple lines of business.


Scalable access models can support quality initiatives across geographically diverse populations without relying on a single engagement approach.

## Preparing for future quality improvement and total cost of care priorities


The direction of quality measurement is becoming increasingly clear. NCQA continues to advance digital quality measurement and ECDS reporting. CMS continues to tie Medicare advantage and Special Needs Plans performance to CMS Star Ratings and quality bonus payments. Medicaid quality reporting is moving toward greater standardization and public transparency, in addition to quality withholds.


For organizations preparing for 2027-2029 quality performance, the opportunity is straightforward. Future quality performance will be shaped by the actions organizations take for the rest of 2026 and early 2027, as the patients who drive future performance and population health initiatives are often identifiable today.


Lab-enabled gaps in care strategies help you move earlier, act with better data, and make it easier for members to complete the tests that close critical care gaps. That means less time chasing follow-ups at year-end and more time focusing on the people and measures that need it most.


That's the difference a year-round strategy makes.
